shipped_originals.title_o: Impulsive choice and pre‐exposure to delays: iv. effects of delay‐ and immediacy‐exposure training relative to maturational changes in impulsivity
shipped_originals.authors_o: Renee Renda; Rung; Hinnenkamp; Lenzini; Madden

blind_target.title: Effects of immediate-reinforcement training on delay discounting behavior in rats
blind_target.evidence_quote:
Experimental work investigating possible causal rela-

tions between impulsive choice and extended experience

with immediate reinforcement is limited, but some work

suggests that experience with immediate reinforcement

may subsequently increase impulsive choice or blunt matu-

rational decreases in impulsive choice in a delay-discounting
paradigm (Fox, 2022; Fox etal., 2019; Renda etal., 2018;

Smith etal., 2022). It was the goal of the work presented

here to expand on this body of research by testing eﬀects

of an immediate reinforcement intervention that was 50%

longer in duration, included approximately twice as many

immediate reinforcement training trials, and employed twice

the sample, than previous work. In doing so, we hoped to

test the limits and generality of previously reported results.
blind_target.outcome_quote:
A group of rats was exposed to an immediate (no-delay)-

reinforcement intervention and subsequent delay discounting

behavior was modestly, but statistically signiﬁcantly, more

impulsive compared to a control group. This is consistent

with previous work (Fox, 2022; Fox etal., 2019; Renda

etal., 2018; Smith etal., 2022), and with the conclusion
that prolonged exposure to immediate reinforcement may

have just modest impacts on subsequent impulsive choice,

compared to relatively larger impacts of exposure to delayed

reinforcement. This was true in the present experiment
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The introduction identifies the set of prior immediate-reinforcement findings whose generality is tested; the discussion explicitly reports consistency with every named member of that set. Modest magnitude is not framed as failure.

shipped_originals.title_o: Trajectories of the effects of sad mood induction procedures (MIPs) (Master’s Thesis)

blind_target.authors: Gillies, J. C. P., & Dozois, D. J. A.
blind_target.title: How long do mood induction procedure (MIP) primes really last? Implications for cognitive vulnerability research.
blind_target.evidence_quote: The two dissertation studies aimed to test the reproducibility of findings from the original study (Gillies, 2018; Gillies & Dozois, 2021) by conducting an exact replication and extending the study design to address the three additional questions listed above.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Statistical analyses of data from these studies revealed results that largely support findings from the original study. That is, the MIPs were often ineffective for a substantial percentage of participants and induced sadness diminished quickly, often within 6 min.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The lay summary gives an overall supportive verdict across both studies. The thesis and subsequent article report the same original sample, but the thesis uniquely reports the latent growth analyses; both are explicitly retested.

shipped_originals.title_o: Climate Schools: Alcohol Module: Cross-Validation of a School-Based Prevention Programme for Alcohol Misuse

blind_target.evidence_quote: This study aimed to replicate research behind Climate Schools: Alcohol and Cannabis course among a large cohort of adolescents.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Abstract explicitly reports replicating alcohol effects but names no original paper or uniquely bounded set of papers. It does not establish which findings from which original were re-tested, so a per-original verdict cannot be assigned. An unresolved target placeholder represents missing identification, not a claim that only one original exists.
